entries.test: Compare OpenAI's Azure inference expenses with the cited reported revenues for CY2024 and H1 CY2025.
entries.note: “It seems” qualifies a concrete numerical comparison with a shared public test.

entries.test: Compare publicly disclosed inference expense records for the relevant periods with the inference costs previously reported by the publications he identifies.
entries.note: “I believe” introduces an asserted factual discrepancy, rather than a claim solely about his private beliefs. The underlying documents need not already be public for the claim to be checkable.

entries.test: Check OpenAI's inference expenses through Q3 CY2025 and its CY2025 cash-flow reconciliation against the reported $9 billion annual cash-burn projection.
entries.note: The spending figure and accounting comparison are checkable. Accrual expenses and cash burn are different measures, so the figures alone do not establish an inconsistency.
He reports his inability to identify a path or justification, without firmly predicting that revenue will fall short. Actual 2025 revenue cannot establish what path he could see when writing.

entries.test: Compare the documents' inference-spending and implied-revenue figures with the earlier published figures for the corresponding periods.
entries.note: The numerical discrepancy is checkable. His wondering about industry costs adds no definite industry-wide claim.

entries.test: Compare OpenAI's inference costs per equivalent workload with customer firms' costs of using its models and the prices OpenAI charges for those workloads.
entries.note: The conditional cost comparison concerns present economics, so it is not a conditional forecast. The suggestion that price increases could be necessary is speculative and supplies no firm prediction.
